title: Package tools
description: Replay one job, installing the small tree program, checking it and removing it, with apt and dpkg on Debian, dnf and rpm on Fedora, yum on AlmaLinux, zypper on openSUSE and apk on Alpine.
intro: Every distribution family has its own package format and tools, but the job is the same. These commands really ran on each distribution, logged in as root. Compare how each tool asks the same questions: what's available, install it, is it installed, which package owns this file, remove it.
takeaways: Debian and its derivatives use `.deb` packages: `dpkg` installs, lists and queries single packages, and `apt` (or the older, script-friendly `apt-get`) fetches them from repositories with their dependencies. `apt update` refreshes the package lists first.

Red Hat-based distributions use `.rpm` packages: `rpm` queries and installs single files, and `dnf` fetches from repositories. On current Enterprise Linux, `yum` is a link to dnf and takes the same commands.
openSUSE and SUSE Linux Enterprise also use RPM packages, with `zypper` as the repository tool; `rpm -q` works there too.
Alpine Linux uses `apk`: `apk add` installs, `apk del` removes, `apk info` describes.
`dpkg -l name` and `rpm -q name` ask whether a package is installed; `dpkg -L name` lists its files, and `dpkg -S file` or `rpm -qf file` names the package a file belongs to.

scenes.title: Debian: apt and dpkg
scenes.text: On Debian 13, root refreshes the package lists, searches, installs `tree`, asks dpkg about it, and removes it with `apt-get`.

notes.apt-update: This only refreshes the lists of available packages; it installs nothing.
notes.dpkg-l: `ii` in the first column means desired: install, status: installed.

questions.prompt: Which tool did the actual unpacking during `apt install`?
questions.why: apt downloads the `.deb` file and resolves dependencies, then hands the file to dpkg, which unpacks and sets it up. The `.deb` file name shows in the output.

questions.prompt: Where did the `tree` program itself get installed?
questions.why: `dpkg -L` lists every file a package installed. Programs from the distribution go to `/usr/bin`; `/usr/local` is for software you build yourself.

scenes.title: Fedora: dnf and rpm
scenes.text: On Fedora 43, root installs `tree` with dnf, queries it with rpm, and removes it.

notes.dnf-install: dnf refreshed the repository metadata on its own before installing; on Debian, that is the separate `apt update`.

questions.prompt: Which command tells you which package the file `/usr/bin/tree` belongs to on Fedora?
questions.why: `-q` queries the package database and `-f` asks by file. `dpkg -S` is the Debian equivalent.

scenes.title: AlmaLinux: yum
scenes.text: Exam 010-160 lists `yum`. On AlmaLinux 10, a rebuild of Red Hat Enterprise Linux, root installs and removes `tree` with it, then looks at what `yum` is.

questions.why: dnf replaced yum, and the name stays as a link so old commands and scripts keep working.

scenes.title: openSUSE: zypper
scenes.text: On openSUSE Leap 16.0, root installs `tree` with zypper, checks it with rpm, and removes it.

notes.zypper-install: `--non-interactive` answered the `Continue?` question with its default, yes.

distractors: zypper installs rpm as a compatibility layer
rpm is part of every Linux distribution
questions.why: SUSE uses the RPM format like Red Hat, with its own repository tool, zypper.

scenes.title: Alpine: apk
scenes.text: On Alpine Linux 3.22, root adds `tree`, asks apk about it, and deletes it.

questions.prompt: Which apk subcommand removed the package?
questions.why: apk uses `add` and `del`. Its output calls the step purging, but the subcommand is `del`.
